title: 10.2 Small Group · Group 1
contentObjective: With my small group, I can find the volume of a rectangular prism, including ones with fractional edge lengths, using base area × height — one step at a time, with support.
languageObjective: I can talk through each step out loud using a sentence frame and the lesson's key words.

noticeAndWonder.context: Is it always true that a cube is a rectangular prism? This prism is built from cubes that are each ½ inch on every edge.
wonderStarters: I wonder what would happen if…

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Choosing a Time-Capsule Box
revealWordProblem.text: Your class is choosing a box for the time capsule. The store sells three rectangular-prism boxes: a Small box that is 2 ft × 1 ft × 1 ft, a Medium box that is 2 ft × 1.5 ft × 1 ft, and a Large box that is 2 ft × 2 ft × 1.5 ft. Compute the volume of each box in cubic feet. Which box should the class buy if they need to fit at least 5 cubic feet of items? Explain how you decided.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Small: V = 2 × 1 × 1 = 2 ft³. Medium: V = 2 × 1.5 × 1 = 3 ft³. Large: V = 2 × 2 × 1.5 = 6 ft³. The class should buy the Large box because only its volume, 6 ft³, is at least 5 ft³.

turnAndTalk.question: Your time capsule is 2 ft long, 1.5 ft wide, and 1 ft tall — one edge is a fraction. Does having a fractional edge change how you find the volume? Why or why not?
turnAndTalk.kernel: You still multiply length × width × height even when an edge is a fraction or decimal.

stems.en: A fractional edge ___ change the method because I still multiply ___ × ___ × ___.
stems.es: Una arista fraccionaria ___ cambia el método porque sigo multiplicando ___ × ___ × ___.

stems.en: The volume of the capsule is ___ ft³.
stems.es: El volumen de la cápsula es ___ ft³.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students explain the formula stays the same (V = l × w × h = 2 × 1.5 × 1 = 3 ft³) and that a fractional edge just means multiplying with a fraction or decimal.
turnAndTalk.extend: How could you use base area × height to find the same volume, and why does that give the same answer as l × w × h?
extendStems: Base area × height gives the same volume because base area is ___.
First I find the base area ___ × ___ = ___, then multiply by the height ___.

turnAndTalk.question: Capsule A (2 × 1.5 × 1) and Capsule B (3 × 1 × 1) both have a volume of 3 ft³. How did your multiplication produce the same volume from different dimensions?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Different dimensions can multiply to the same product, so the volumes match.

stems.en: Both capsules have V = ___ ft³ because ___ × ___ × ___ = ___ × ___ × ___.
stems.es: Ambas cápsulas tienen V = ___ ft³ porque ___ × ___ × ___ = ___ × ___ × ___.

stems.en: The dimensions are different but the ___ is the same.
stems.es: Las dimensiones son diferentes pero el ___ es el mismo.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students show 2 × 1.5 × 1 = 3 and 3 × 1 × 1 = 3, and explain that the same product means equal volume even with different shapes.
turnAndTalk.extend: If two capsules have the same volume but different dimensions, which would you choose to store long, flat objects, and why?
extendStems: I would choose Capsule ___ because its dimensions ___.
Same volume does not mean same usefulness because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: A fish tank is 24 in long, 12 in wide, and 16 in tall, and one gallon takes about 231 cubic inches. Talk through how you would find how many gallons it holds.
turnAndTalk.kernel: Find the volume with V = l × w × h, then divide by 231 to convert to gallons.

stems.en: The tank's volume is ___ in³ because 24 × 12 × 16 = ___.
stems.es: El volumen del tanque es ___ in³ porque 24 × 12 × 16 = ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students compute 4608 in³, then divide by 231 to get about 20 gallons, and explain that dividing converts cubic inches into gallons.
turnAndTalk.extend: Why does the answer come out to about 20 gallons instead of an exact whole number, and how would you decide whether to round up or down for filling the tank?
extendStems: The answer is not exact because ___.
To fill the tank safely I would round ___ because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: A classmate says a 5 × 3 × 2.5 m prism has volume 5 × 5.5 = 27.5 m³. How do you find and explain their mistake?
turnAndTalk.kernel: They added 3 + 2.5 instead of multiplying; the correct volume is 5 × 7.5 = 37.5 m³.

stems.en: The mistake is that they ___ instead of multiplying 3 × 2.5.
stems.es: El error es que ___ en lugar de multiplicar 3 × 2.5.

stems.en: The correct volume is ___ m³ because 3 × 2.5 = ___, then 5 × ___ = ___.
stems.es: El volumen correcto es ___ m³ porque 3 × 2.5 = ___, luego 5 × ___ = ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Students identify the added-instead-of-multiplied error, compute 3 × 2.5 = 7.5, and conclude the correct volume is 37.5 m³.
turnAndTalk.extend: What general rule about the volume formula does this mistake break, and how could a quick estimate have caught it?
extendStems: The mistake breaks the rule that volume always uses ___.
An estimate would catch it because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice on Volume of Rectangular Prisms, what strategy did you use when a problem felt tricky?
turnAndTalk.kernel: A fractional edge does not change the rule: still multiply length × width × height.

stems.en: Both capsules have V = ___ ft³ because ___ × ___ × ___ = ___ × ___ × ___.
stems.es: Ambas cápsulas tienen V = ___ ft³ porque ___ × ___ × ___ = ___ × ___ × ___.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming a specific strategy tied to 6.GR.2 — not just "I multiplied." They should connect steps to the key idea.
turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who made the common mistake from today's lesson? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ first because ___.
The mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

launch.narrative: This is your support small group for Lesson 10.2. We're going to slow this down and build it together, one step at a time. You can ask a question any time — that's what this group is for.
launch.contextImage: Students gathered around a rectangular box time capsule with items to place inside
noticePrompts: What are the three measurements of the time capsule?
What does volume measure — length, area, or space inside?
How is volume different from area?
wonderPrompts: What if we made the capsule taller but narrower — would the volume change?
What units do we use for volume versus area?

conceptIntro.heading: Let's build it together — How do we find volume when an edge is a fraction?
conceptIntro.intro: Volume is the space inside a box. The rule V = length × width × height stays the same even when one edge is a fraction or decimal. You can also use volume = base area × height. We'll walk through a worked example, try one together, then you'll try a few with hints right there when you need them.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: A fractional edge does not change the rule: still multiply length × width × height.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: My capsule is 2 ft long, 1.5 ft wide, and 1 ft tall. I write V = length × width × height.
I put in the numbers: V = 2 × 1.5 × 1.
So the volume is 3 ft³. A fractional edge like 1.5 did not change my steps at all.

weDo.title: Let's try together
lines: Now try a box that is 4 long, 2 wide, and 0.5 tall. What formula do we use?
Put in the numbers: V = 4 × 2 × 0.5. What is 4 × 2?
We got 8. Now multiply 8 × 0.5 (that means half of 8). What is the volume?
Yes, V = 4 cubic units. The decimal edge just made the answer a little smaller.
Sentence frame — say it with me: "The multiples/steps I need are ___ , and the answer is ___ ."

youDo.title: Now you try — with support
lines: Try the practice problems below. The hint button is right there whenever you get stuck — use it, that's smart.
Remember the key idea: A fractional edge does not change the rule: still multiply length × width × height..

explore.instructions: Quick warm-up together: Calculate the volume of each possible time capsule design. Use V = l × w × h.

discourse.prompt: Capsules A and B have the same volume (3 ft³) but different dimensions. Why? Which design would you choose and why?
discourse.sentenceFrame: Capsules A and B both have V = ___ because ___ × ___ × ___ = ___ × ___ × ___. I'd choose ___ because ___.

approaching.stem: What is the volume of a rectangular prism with l = 4 in, w = 3 in, h = 5 in?
approaching.explanation: V = l × w × h = 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 cubic inches.
choiceFeedback: Are you adding the dimensions? Volume multiplies all edges: length × width × height.
Check the units. Area is square units (²), volume is cubic units (³).
Check your calculation. Re-read the problem carefully.
hints: Spot the three edges: l = 4 in, w = 3 in, h = 5 in. Volume fills the whole box, so all three matter.
Use V = l × w × h and remember the answer needs cubic units (in³), not square units.
Multiply 4 × 3 = 12 for the base, then multiply that result by the height, 5 inches.

approaching.stem: A box has a volume of 36 cm³. Its length is 6 cm and width is 3 cm. What is the height?
choiceFeedback: That number is the length given in the problem — divide volume by the full base area to find height.
That's the width from the problem, not the height — divide the volume by length × width instead.
Check your division — find the full base area (length × width) before dividing into the volume.
hints: You're given the volume (36 cm³) plus two edges (6 cm and 3 cm). The height is what's missing.
Work backward: divide the volume by the base area (length × width) to uncover the height.
Find the base area first: 6 × 3 = 18 cm². Then ask what number times 18 gives 36.

approaching.stem: How is volume different from area?
choices: Volume measures 3D space (cubic units); area measures 2D surface (square units)
Volume uses square units; area uses cubic units
Volume only applies to cubes; area applies to all shapes
approaching.explanation: Volume measures the space inside a 3D shape (cubic units like in³). Area measures a flat 2D surface (square units like in²).
choiceFeedback: The units are swapped here — think about which measurement fills 3D space and which covers a flat surface.
Volume isn't just for cubes — it applies to any 3D shape, like prisms and pyramids too.
These two measurements are different — one covers a flat surface, and one fills a 3D space.
hints: Think dimensions: area covers a flat 2D surface, while volume fills a 3D space.
Match each measurement to its unit: flat surfaces get square units (²), filled space gets cubic units (³).
Picture a rug (flat) versus a fish tank (filled). Decide which is area and which is volume, then check each choice.

approaching.title: approaching — Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Dimensions
workedExample.work: A box is 5 in long, 4 in wide, and 2 in tall.

approaching.correctWork: The student added the dimensions instead of multiplying. Volume means multiply: V = 5 × 4 × 2 = 20 × 2 = 40 cubic in.
hints: Check Step 3: should you add the dimensions or multiply them?
Volume is length × width × height. Multiply: 5 × 4 × 2 = 40 cubic in, not 11.

approaching.instructions: Find the volume of each rectangular prism.
approaching.hint: Use the formula V = length × width × height for each row.
hints: Each row lists a length, width, and height. The blank Volume cell needs a number with cubic units.
For every row use V = l × w × h: multiply the first two numbers, then multiply by the third.
Row 1: multiply 8 × 5 = 40 first, then multiply by the height, 2. Include in³ in your answer.

onLevel.stem: Two boxes: Box A is 10 × 5 × 4 inches. Box B is 8 × 6 × 5 inches. Which has more volume and by how much?
onLevel.explanation: Box A: 10 × 5 × 4 = 200 in³. Box B: 8 × 6 × 5 = 240 in³. Box B is bigger by 40 in³.
choiceFeedback: Recheck which box's volume is larger — recalculate both totals before comparing.
You picked the right box, but recheck the subtraction to find the exact difference.
These two volumes aren't equal — calculate each box's volume and compare the totals.
hints: This asks two things: which box holds more AND by how many cubic inches — so find both volumes first.
Compute each volume with V = l × w × h, then subtract the smaller total from the larger.
Box A: 10 × 5 = 50, then × 4. Box B: 8 × 6 = 48, then × 5. Compare the two totals.

onLevel.title: onLevel — Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Dimensions
workedExample.work: A box is 6 in long, 4 in wide, and 1/2 in tall.

workedExample.label: Calculate
workedExample.work: V = 6 × 4 × 1/2, and the student dropped the 1/2: V = 6 × 4 = 24 cubic in

onLevel.correctWork: The student ignored the fractional edge of 1/2 in. A fractional edge still counts: V = 6 × 4 × 1/2 = 24 × 1/2 = 12 cubic in.
hints: Check Step 3: did the student use the 1/2 in height in the multiplication?
A fractional edge does not change the rule. Multiply all three: 6 × 4 × 1/2 = 12 cubic in, not 24.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Volume of Rectangular Prisms is rounding a fractional edge length to the nearest whole number before multiplying, instead of using the exact fraction or decimal. For a box that is 2 ft × 1.5 ft × 1 ft, a student might round 1.5 down to 1 and compute 2 × 1 × 1 = 2 ft³, but the correct volume uses the exact edge length: 2 × 1.5 × 1 = 3 ft³ — a full cubic foot larger. Before you submit, ask: 'Did I multiply using the exact fractional or decimal edge length, or did I round it off first?'

exitTicket.stem: Quick check — you've got this: A rectangular prism has l = 7 ft, w = 2 ft, h = 3 ft. What is the volume?
exitTicket.explanation: V = 7 × 2 × 3 = 42 cubic feet. Remember: volume uses cubic units (ft³).
choiceFeedback: Check your calculation. Re-read the problem carefully.
Check the units. Area is square units (²), volume is cubic units (³).
Are you adding the dimensions? Volume multiplies all edges: length × width × height.
hints: Note the edges: l = 7 ft, w = 2 ft, h = 3 ft — and remember volume answers use cubic units (ft³).
Apply V = l × w × h, multiplying all three edges, and pick an answer with cubic units.
Multiply 7 × 2 = 14 first, then multiply that result by the height, 3 feet.
